title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation fraud in which AI-generated content was used to fabricate a realistic-seeming interview between two named public figures, neither of whom participated. The failure occurred entirely outside any legitimate AI deployment: bad actors used generative tools to produce convincing text, then published it to promote an unlicensed financial platform. The fabricated exchange included specific dramatic details, such as one participant leaving the room, that gave it the texture of authentic journalism.

The mechanism that makes this fraud effective is the same one that makes it hard to catch before it spreads: polished, contextually plausible content no longer requires significant resources or skill to produce. There is no deployment pipeline with a human reviewer to intercept the output, because the content is produced and distributed entirely by the scammers themselves. Catching it requires either platform-level detection of synthetic media or reader-level verification against primary sources, neither of which operates automatically.

What is established here is a regulator's warning and its own removal statistics, not a court finding of fraud against any named individual or entity. The scale figures, including the percentage increases in phishing and fake investment platforms, come from ASIC's own research and have not been independently adjudicated.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featured a fabricated interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock discussing Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The article depicted an increasingly heated exchange where Bullock supposedly stormed out over Kohler's questions about the platform's alleged market exploitation algorithm. However, this interview never actually occurred. The scam represents a growing trend of AI-generated investment fraud that Australian financial regulators say is becoming more prevalent and sophisticated.

The corporate watchdog ASIC released research showing a significant rise in these deceptive schemes, removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams jumped 279 percent, while fake investment platforms increased by 151 percent. Kohler ranks among the most commonly impersonated Australians, alongside Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, politicians like Pauline Hanson and Angus Taylor, and wealthy individuals including Gina Rinehart and Dick Smith. ASIC warns consumers to verify financial services licenses through its public registers and avoid websites lacking verifiable credentials. The regulator advises that polished content and familiar branding do not guarantee legitimacy.
